items.summary: Chee Wee Kiong, a former permanent secretary for foreign affairs in Singapore, argues that the city-state acted responsibly and diligently regarding allegations linking it to the diversion of advanced Nvidia chips and AI infrastructure to China. He contends these narratives are baseless, asserting instead that Singapore launched its own independent investigation into potentially fraudulent declarations about equipment destinations within its jurisdiction—rather than acting as an instrument of U.S. export controls—and subsequently charged multiple individuals where evidence supported criminal action. In the Megaspeed matter involving senior executive Alice Huang, authorities interviewed her and restricted her travel for over six months before concluding that available evidence was insufficient to sustain a case; she was released but received a stern warning and future entry restrictions, which Kiong frames as adherence to rule of law rather than letting someone go. He emphasizes Singapore's repeated requests for additional information from suppliers and U.S. agencies such as the Department of Justice and FBI, noting officials were unable to obtain evidence needed to advance certain lines of inquiry or establish a complete evidentiary chain. Kiong also disputes common misconceptions about Singapore's role in semiconductor supply chains, distinguishing between physical chip diversion and remote access to computing capacity via cloud services, data centers, and leased compute resources, while correcting the widely repeated claim that roughly 20% of Nvidia's business passes through Singapore by explaining that revenue attribution differs from actual physical shipments. He concludes that export controls are only as effective as international cooperation supporting them and that blaming an intermediary jurisdiction for failing to prove facts external actors were unwilling or unable to provide misses the broader challenge posed by global technology network complexity.
items.title: Former Foreign Affairs Official Defends Singapore's Handling of Nvidia Chip Allegations

items.summary: Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said Singapore will keep negotiating with the United States to lower tariffs that could hit about $9.4 billion worth of its exports, noting any deal would require compromises on both sides (q1, q2). The proposed Section 301 tariff rate of up to 20% would raise the effective duty on Singapore goods from 7.8% to 10.3%, and USTR Jamieson Greer offered to consider cutting it to 10% if Singapore reaches an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (q3, q4, q5, q6, q10). Gan expressed surprise at the US trade office's actions, which followed a 168-page investigation report citing structural excess capacity in Singapore's manufacturing and electronics sectors as well as its Central Provident Fund (q14). The USTR conducted this Section 301 review against 16 trading partners including Japan, the EU and South Korea; tariffs could take effect in early 2027. Separately, some Singapore exports face US sectoral tariffs of 25% to 50% on steel, aluminium, copper and automotive parts (q21, q22). The article notes that despite a growing bilateral trade surplus with the United States — $27 billion in 2024 rising to $33 billion in 2025 — Singapore remains the third-largest Asian investor in the US behind Japan and South Korea.
items.title: Singapore's $9.4 Billion in Exports Threatened by Proposed US Tariffs

items.summary: Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani said Malaysia will continue negotiations with the United States through the first quarter of 2027 to keep overall tariffs on Malaysian goods at or below 19%, which was agreed under the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART). He told reporters that the US had indicated a tariff range of between 18% and 25% for Malaysia, but argued any additional measures must not push the total above 19%. This includes a finalized 10% forced-labour tariff already factored into the ceiling. Johari said Malaysia's position remains unchanged despite the US excess-capacity assessment, which he disputed on the grounds that Malaysia does not have structural excess capacity; meanwhile, iron and steel sectors could face scrutiny while semiconductors were excluded from the review at this stage. The proposed tariffs relate to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, under which Malaysia is one of 14 economies facing rates ranging from 15% to 35%, alongside China, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Japan and the European Union.
items.title: Malaysia to seek 19% tariff ceiling in US talks until Q1 2027

items.summary: Eighteen-year-old Jaime Chua Xin Jie argues that tuition centres should disclose the frequency and cost of additional classes before enrolment, obtain explicit consent before billing families, and allow parents to decline these sessions without financial penalty. The contributor notes that some centres introduce extra holiday or pre-exam classes—potentially doubling usual fees—that may not be clearly disclosed at enrolment and are sometimes billed automatically. Chua also contends that the value of such sessions warrants scrutiny, citing cases where students pay for a full session to sit a mock paper they could complete at home. To reduce reliance on tuition overall, the writer suggests the Ministry of Education expand revision resources on the Student Learning Space, including examination-paper walkthroughs, so all students have greater access to structured support.
items.title: Singaporean Teenager Calls for Scrutiny of Tuition Centres' Additional Class Offerings

items.summary: An investigation has found that undisclosed use of generative AI affected at least 25 court cases in 2026, according to a trawl of published judgments by the Bureau of Investigative Journalism shared with the Guardian. The cases span lawyers, police officers, and self-represented litigants misusing the technology — including a high court tax dispute marred by “unacceptable” generative AI hallucinations and references to nonexistent cases; a $21m (£16m) Nigerian oil companies case in which an argument rested on a ruling entirely invented by a hallucinating AI, prompting the judge to warn of relying on unverified AI output; and a grievous bodily harm appeal where an investigating officer created a victim personal statement using Microsoft Copilot with instructions “to achieve the highest sentence and the most tear-jerking VPS.” Judges have also complained that verbose AI-generated documents — such as 60-page submissions versus three pages from human judgment, per Law Society president Brett Dixon — are consuming more time and undermining court backlogs. Supreme Court judge Lord Sales said the court is “increasingly concerned” about AI deskilling the profession, while Civil Justice Council guidance now requires fact witnesses in civil cases to sign a declaration that their statements were not prepared through an AI tool.
items.title: Undisclosed AI Use Affected More Than Two Dozen Court Cases in England and Wales

items.summary: The UK's Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) declined to jointly test Meta's AI assistant, Muse, in its regulatory sandbox after the company only informed it of its plans last month, according to FCA head of innovation Colin Payne. The refusal reportedly stems from concerns about setup time and a desire for more information before committing resources. This dispute unfolds as UK regulators warn that Meta must ensure its AI products comply with consumer protection laws. Payne described agentic tools like Muse—marketed as personal assistants—as 'another force of attack,' noting the FCA wants to understand how these autonomous agents interact with customers, particularly regarding payments and unintended consequences when users have limited understanding of the technology. The concern is heightened because multiple British retailers, including Sainsbury's, Marks & Spencer, Ocado, Debenhams Group, and Currys, are reportedly working with Meta to integrate Muse into their sites. More than 10 million users had set up Muse in North America since its September launch, prompting UK watchdogs to brace for significant adoption given that many British consumers already use Meta's Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp products. Payne emphasized the need to observe what Muse will do if it becomes equally popular in the UK. The Information Commissioner's Office stressed the importance of users understanding and controlling how their personal data is used by Muse, while the Competition and Markets Authority had already required Meta to adapt its terms for UK consumers—mandating that Meta exercise 'reasonable skill and care/professional diligence' when providing the service, with documents acknowledging outputs may be inaccurate. The CMA stated it would not hesitate to act if concerns arise.
items.title: UK Regulators Warn Meta Over AI Assistant Muse Amid Testing Dispute

items.summary: The nearly completed East Side Coastal Resiliency Project in lower Manhattan relies heavily on flood protection systems hidden beneath the rebuilt John V. Lindsay East River Park, including a 2-foot-thick concrete wall anchored by deep steel structures and sealed against seepage using jet grouting to inject cement-based material into the ground. The system is designed to hold back flooding up to 16.5 feet above sea level, with engineers adding two extra feet of protection for a total capacity of 18.5 feet in case their projections were wrong, according to Joseph G. Lione, associate commissioner for coastal resiliency at the city's Department of Design and Construction. The project was developed after Hurricane Sandy devastated Lower Manhattan in 2012 and aims to protect about 110,000 East Side residents; it costs $1.45 billion, began construction in 2020, and is expected to finish in 2027, with the city reporting that over $1 billion has already been completed. Community advocates have continued opposing the redesign since its announcement in 2018, raising concerns about tree removal—though retired biology professor Amy Burkoff's measurements showed most of the compared trees had grown between 2015 and 2021—and about reduced shade from newly planted trees that are expected to take decades to mature.
items.title: Hidden Floodwalls and Underground Barriers Protect Lower Manhattan's East River Park

items.summary: The Swiss Federal Council amended the Energy Promotion Ordinance (EnFV) to raise one-time payments for photovoltaic systems in the below-30 kW and 30-kW-to-below-100-kW categories by CHF 40/kW, with the power-based contribution capped at 30% of reference-system investment costs. Building-integrated PV systems qualify for an additional payment of about 10%. The Council also raised the high one-time payment (HEIV) rate to CHF 550/kW for systems below 150 kW that do not consume their own electricity, with a contribution cap at 60% of reference-system investment costs; building-integrated systems are excluded from this additional scheme. Industry association Swissolar welcomed the changes as further incentives for solar on apartment buildings, commercial properties, and agricultural buildings but criticized omissions: it called for simplifying price regulation under collective self-consumption schemes (ZEV), fully using statutory grid-charge reductions for local electricity communities (LEG), requiring default suppliers to offer dynamic tariffs, capping metering charges, and raising the cap on support for strengthening grid connection lines from CHF 50/kW to CHF 100/kW. The Council also revised other ordinances: under the Energy Ordinance it set financial security at least 1.5 times estimated compensatory-measure costs; abolished individually calculated fees for ZEV and LEG schemes; simplified transmission-line planning by directly determining corridors rather than designating areas, per revisions to the Planning Approval Procedure ordinance implementing an Electricity Act amendment; and revised the CO2 Ordinance so only direct geothermal use receives support while solar thermal process-heat support ends. The article presents these as Federal Council decisions and Swissolar's reactions.
items.title: Switzerland raises solar incentives below 100 kW

items.summary: Mexico's General Directorate of Environmental and Risk Impact (DGIRA), part of the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat), has granted conditional environmental approval for the 621.17 MWp Cerro Colorado solar project, which developer Desarrollos y Soluciones Energéticas Eirene plans to build in Sayula de Alemán and Texistepec municipalities in Veracruz state. The plant will comprise 941,166 solar modules each rated at 660 W, along with 1,803 Huawei SUN2000-330KTL-H1 inverters each rated at 330 kW, supported by a 34.5 kV medium-voltage network and three 34.5/230 kV step-up substations. It will cover 1,062.62 hectares across North, Central and South sections, with permanent infrastructure occupying 296.90 hectares (27.94% of the total) while 763.89 hectares remain free of infrastructure; the design also includes new internal roads totaling 19.86 km plus a further 13.67 km of existing roads. Environmental conditions require full conservation of 40.89 hectares of secondary vegetation in medium-height evergreen rainforest, alongside programs to monitor wildlife, conserve habitats and ecological connectivity, and restore riverbanks and riparian areas. The authorization allows two years for site preparation and construction, 30 years for operation and maintenance, and nine months for decommissioning; the environmental documentation references battery energy storage systems but does not specify their capacity. Eirene submitted the regional environmental impact statement on Feb. 19, 2026, though this approval does not exempt the developer from obtaining other federal, state and municipal permits.
items.title: Mexico conditionally approves Veracruz solar plant

items.summary: The 21st edition of European Sustainable Energy Week (EUSEW) will run from June 23 to 25, 2027, under the theme 'Powering a resilient future for Europe,' taking place in Brussels and online. The EUSEW Policy Conference is expected to feature more than 50 sessions covering clean energy, energy efficiency, and innovation as part of efforts to strengthen Europe's energy security while reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels. Calls for breakout session proposals are open with a deadline of January 21, 2027, offering three formats: policy, solution, and workshop sessions. Applications and nominations for the EUSEW Awards—recognizing contributions in Local Energy Action, Women in Energy, and SMEs Driving Energy Efficiency—are due by January 28, 2027. An online Info Session is scheduled for Wednesday, December 9, from 11:00 to 12:30 CET, during which European Commission representatives will present the event's theme, milestones, and participation details.
items.title: European Sustainable Energy Week 2027 to be held in Brussels

items.summary: A professional e-bike tester who rides for work and owns no car names the FoldyLock Elite 110 as his single best bike lock, calling it “the world’s strongest folding lock” after living with it daily. The reviewer states he would choose this one if forced to use only a single lock, though he also recommends using two locks of different styles for theft prevention; in practice he pairs the FoldyLock Elite 110 as his primary with a SeatyLock Mason 220 U-lock (rated Sold Secure Diamond) as secondary. He reports that both folding locks are identical in strength and security to each other, confirmed by ART—the only folding locks ever to earn its top-tier 3-star rating on the five-point scale—and also holds Sold Secure GOLD status; he notes this was achieved three years ago with no other company matching it since a folding lock. He describes the Elite’s protected rivets against nut-splitter attacks and squeaks, holster-locking that prevents bounce-outs, corrosion-resistant coating, and mounting via flexible straps on his fork despite adding 1.9 kg (4.1 lb). On value he cites an MSRP of $145 with a Black Friday price of $119, arguing the durable lock is worth even full price versus top-tier locks costing $200 or more.
items.title: FoldyLock Elite 110 Review

items.summary: On Monday Nvidia's board unanimously voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO in a stunning reversal of his ouster two weeks earlier over admissions of extramarital affairs. The decision followed pressure from President Trump, who repeatedly advocated for Huang's return and dialed into the company's Sunday board meeting; the White House stated “We have to protect our geniuses.” Nvidia's stock rebounded on Monday after having tanked more than 10% during his departure, gaining nearly $1tn in market value. Trump, a shareholder who owns shares in the chip maker, reportedly made up to $15m with the surge that day.
items.title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang after board reversal, sending stock sharply higher

items.summary: A consumer in Panchkula, Haryana (the source attributes the case's origin to a shop in Kasipur, Uttarakhand) bought an iPhone 14 on February 19, 2023 from a Panipat store and reported display problems within three days; AppleCare replaced it with a new phone on February 22, 2023. On November 14, 2023 the customer noticed speaker failure and overheating at an authorized service center, where staff initially said the device was under warranty and would be fixed within a week. Service-center representatives reportedly cited a defective microphone grille as the cause of damage and demanded Rs 79,000 for repairs on November 21; after further inspection and cleaning on December 1, they again blamed the microphone grille and asked for Rs 42,900 (the figure Apple ultimately pressed in its claim). On November 12, the Panchkula District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission ordered Apple India to repair the phone free of cost within 45 days and pay compensation plus legal costs totaling Rs 5,500. The commission reached this decision after reviewing service records, messages, and other documents; it found that Apple failed to produce any expert technician report establishing that customer negligence caused the damage, and rejected Apple's argument that physical damage fell outside its one-year warranty coverage.
items.title: Haryana Consumer Commission Orders Apple to Repair iPhone 14 Free and Pay Rs 5,500

items.summary: IBM has decided to end US visa and green card sponsorship for most positions in its consulting division, according to Bloomberg. The move leaves affected foreign employees with two options: relocate abroad for an internal role or leave the company by the end of 2026. IBM Consulting is the firm's largest division, employing more than 150,000 people, and has reportedly communicated the change to managers. Employees impacted have been given three weeks to decide whether to accept an overseas position or depart the organization. The decision could significantly affect Indian professionals working in the United States on H-1B visas.
items.title: IBM to End H-1B and Green Card Sponsorship for Most Consulting Jobs

items.summary: A study by João Tampellini (forthcoming in the Journal of Development Economics) uses the post–US Civil War migration of Confederados to São Paulo state as evidence that immigrants' long-run influence depends on both who arrives and what institutions they find. Between 5,000 and 10,000 US Southerners migrated to Brazil after their defeat, many settling in then-frontier areas; about a third came from the top decile of pre-war wealth distribution. They brought agricultural knowledge, business experience, and capital scarce in the region, and they arrived with strong cultural views including racial prejudices. The study follows these municipalities using census data spanning 1836 to 2010 plus archival records, comparing them at each point against other São Paulo municipalities (which share institutions) while controlling for suitability to cotton, coffee, sugar, and tobacco.
items.title: Confederate migrants industrialised a poor region of Brazil, but only their churches and schools endured

items.summary: A Bank of England study using a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) model calibrated to UK data from 1997–2025 finds that the rise of non-bank financial institutions does not weaken conventional monetary policy, because borrowing costs still pass smoothly through wholesale funding and bond markets. However, quantitative easing's effect on output depends critically on why the non-bank sector expanded: QE is about 15.4% more powerful under a firm-driven expansion (firms shifting toward market-based finance), while it remains largely unchanged when growth stems from constrained bank lending. The authors attribute this difference to a stronger portfolio-rebalancing channel in the firm-driven case, which is offset by higher bank borrowing costs there.
items.title: Non-bank growth reshapes QE transmission but not interest-rate policy

visual.alt: Bar chart. 2008 (baseline) (Bank lending share in 2008) 60 %; Latest estimate (Bank lending share now) 40 %.

items.summary: On Thursday (Nov 26), Vietnam said it was working with the United States to complete a trade deal as soon as possible, hours after the Trump administration threatened new tariffs that could hit key export industries including clothing and footwear. The manufacturing hub runs the largest trade surplus of any US partner and faces potential tariff rates of 35 per cent on grounds of excessive industrial capacity (q1), which would exceed those of Southeast Asian peers and rank second only to China's among the 14 targeted countries (q2). Vietnam has spent more than a year negotiating with Washington, and industry officials who had expected an agreement in December—when leader To Lam is set to attend a G20 summit in Florida—see the tariff threat as an inducement. Bruno Jaspaert, head of DEEP C Industrial Zones, said he would not rule out a deal over the coming months. Such a trade deal could leave Vietnam with tariffs of 20 per cent (q3), above an existing general duty of 12.5 per cent (q4) and well below the threatened 35 per cent (q5). Competitors in apparel and footwear such as Bangladesh, Cambodia and Indonesia have struck deals for tariffs of 18 per cent (q6). The threats add uncertainty for manufacturers serving the American market; John Cambell of Savills said garments, textiles and footwear producers with significant US exposure would be particularly sensitive to higher costs. Officials noted that months of tariff uncertainty may already have hurt some sectors as production shifted elsewhere and orders dropped. Vietnam also faces a February 28 deadline in a US investigation into intellectual property violations and accusations of functioning as a transit point for Chinese goods, which is especially ominous for the electronics industry that uses large volumes of Chinese-made components.
items.title: Vietnam Pursues US Trade Deal as Tariffs Threaten Clothing, Footwear Exports

visual.alt: Bar chart. Threatened (excessive capacity) (Vietnam threatened) 35 %; Proposed deal outcome (Vietnam proposed) 20 %; Existing general duty (baseline) (Vietnam baseline) 12.5 %; Competitors' agreed deal (Regional competitors) 18 %.

items.summary: On Thursday (Nov 26), China said it reserves the right to take 'necessary measures' after Washington unveiled new tariffs that could reach up to 20 per cent, with Beijing urging the United States to return to dialogue. Commerce ministry spokesman He Yadong called citing 'overcapacity' as a reason for the tariffs a 'pretext for protectionism,' arguing such actions disrupt global supply chains and pose systemic risks to economic growth. The proposed US levies target multiple trading partners including China, the European Union, and Japan, with China among those facing the highest 20-per cent rate; however, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new tariffs fall within existing trade negotiations with Beijing, noting the United States is offering exemptions on around US$30 billion of Chinese goods. The escalation follows Trump's second-term tariffs that at one point saw duties touch 145 per cent, and comes as a Trump–Xi trade ceasefire struck in October 2025 approaches its January expiry after a two-month extension agreed in September.
items.title: China Reserves Right to Take Measures After New US Tariffs

items.summary: Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights and warned it will file for bankruptcy unless short-term financing is secured urgently. The airline announced its precarious position on Thursday, a day after describing its finances as 'critical.' Norse attributes the crisis to surging jet fuel prices that have risen since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, which have also dampened consumer confidence. In a statement to the Oslo stock exchange, the carrier said: 'If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the board's intention to file for bankruptcy.' Norse noted it remains exploring options and was discussing a possible takeover with investors, but cautioned that 'There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found.' The airline, founded in 2021 to fill the space left by Norwegian Air after its budget long-haul operations were abandoned as unviable, operates transatlantic routes from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia with a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 Dreamliners. Norse had earlier launched Project Falcon, a cost-cutting programme aimed at saving $50m (£38m), which included cutting about 75 jobs, moving its headquarters out of Norway to cheaper offices in Latvia, and the departure of founder and chief executive Bjørn Tore Larsen. Affected UK routes include London Gatwick to Orlando, Bangkok and Cape Town, while a winter service from Manchester to Thailand was scheduled to begin next month.
items.title: Norse Atlantic Airways Suspends All Flights Amid Urgent Funding Plea

items.summary: A recent NBER working paper documents five facts about payment stablecoins using wallet-level blockchain data from 2020 to 2025. First, the authors find that stablecoins serve as a transaction currency: onchain volume exceeds Bitcoin's despite a much smaller supply, velocity has risen sharply, and transactions have shifted toward low-value transfers. Second, by using transaction timing to refine exchange-based attribution, they estimate activity is spread across the Americas, Europe, and Asia with fewer cross-regional flows than the standard method implies. Third, estimating a structural cash-management model on holdings data, they find that the costs of accessing stablecoin wallets have fallen since 2023. Fourth, the paper reports that stablecoins are becoming the settlement currency of a fast-growing onchain credit market and that their growth appears to reallocate rather than destroy credit. Fifth, smart contracts are involved in about a third of Ethereum stablecoin transactions and over two thirds of volume, with protocols such as x402 demonstrating sub-cent machine-to-machine payments. The authors conclude that stablecoins behave as tokenized money, with implications for financial markets and regulation.
items.title: Five Facts About Payment Stablecoins

items.summary: The UK has signed an £8bn contract with defence firm Babcock to upgrade its nuclear submarine fleet, a five-year deal Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said would help get the country 'warfighting ready.' The agreement will create 3,000 new jobs and around 2,500 apprentice and graduate roles mainly across Plymouth, Clyde and Bristol. It is part of a wider £26bn investment into the UK's naval bases announced earlier this year.
items.title: UK Signs £8bn Deal to Upgrade Nuclear Submarine Fleet

items.summary: On November 26, 2026, Apple removed Talkie, an artificial intelligence chatbot developed by China's MiniMax (through its Singapore-based subsidiary SUBSUP), from the App Store worldwide after a joint investigation with the UK-based Bureau of Investigative Journalism found potentially harmful interactions between the platform and children. The ABC News report documented accounts from parents in Australia and the US who discovered sexually inappropriate exchanges, as well as verbally abusive content, between their children and AI-generated characters on Talkie. Unlike conventional assistants, Talkie enables simulated personal relationships with virtual characters through text and voice conversations. Although Apple's App Store and Google Play carried an age rating of 18 or above (q3), the service was accessed by thousands of children; ABC News reported that it had been downloaded more than 50 million times on Google Play, where it remained available at the time of reporting (q4). Company documents reviewed by investigators indicated users spent an average of more than 70 minutes a day on Talkie and its Chinese counterpart. This removal marked Apple's second withdrawal of Talkie; an earlier version was removed in 2024 over objectionable user-generated content before MiniMax released a new version in 2025.
items.title: Apple Removes Chinese AI Companion App Talkie Over Child Safety Concerns

items.summary:
An Indian trade body has urged New Delhi to impose retaliatory tariffs of 25 per cent on American goods, warning that Washington's latest tariff proposals could put 500,000 jobs at risk and affect more than US$48 billion worth of Indian exports. Brijesh Goyal, chairman of the Delhi-based Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI), said in a statement shared with CNA on Thursday (Nov 26) that the textile, leather, gems and jewellery, auto components and seafood industries could be severely affected. The CTI had written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi urging him to impose matching tariffs on US imports including minerals, machinery, aircraft equipment, electronics, plastics, chemicals, and iron and steel.

The USTR proposed tariffs of up to 25 per cent on Indian goods over allegations that India produces more than its market needs, potentially falling to 17 per cent if New Delhi reaches a trade deal with Washington. The proposal would account for existing Section 301 duties rather than being added on top; Indian goods already subject to an additional 10 per cent tariff could face up to 25 per cent, not 35 per cent. Certain products including smartphones, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, metals, vehicles and aircraft parts are exempt from the proposed tariffs.

India's Commerce Ministry said it was reviewing the US proposal, reiterating that India had no structural excess manufacturing capacity in any sector and that trade concerns should be addressed through bilateral negotiations. Chandrima Chatterjee of the Confederation of Indian Textile Industry (CITI) warned that frequent tariff changes were creating uncertainty for exporters and overseas buyers, while Rohit Kumar of the India Trade Council said prolonged uncertainty was already affecting US sourcing decisions as buyers shift manufacturing to the United States.

The proposed tariffs have not yet taken effect. Washington is seeking public comments until Jan 5, 2027, ahead of hearings scheduled to begin on Jan 25.
items.title: Indian Trade Body Urges Retaliatory Tariffs on US Goods

visual.alt: Bar chart. Existing Section 301 additional tariff (Section 301 measure (July)) 10 %; Proposed US tariffs on Indian goods (USTR proposal) 25 %; Rate if India reaches a trade deal (Trade-deal scenario) 17 %.

items.summary: Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said the Central Provident Fund (CPF) scheme does not suppress domestic consumption, disputing the United States' claim that Singapore's policies contributed to its structural excess capacity. Speaking Thursday (Nov 26), Mr Gan — also minister for energy, trade and industry — described himself as surprised by US concern over the
items.title: Singapore Rejects US Tariff Justification on CPF as Surprise Levy Looms

items.summary: For the first time, Chinese cities occupied the top three positions in global science rankings: Beijing ranked first as the world's leading science city for 2025, followed by Shanghai and Nanjing. These findings were published in the Nature Index 2026 Science Cities supplement, which measures research output across major cities worldwide based on publications in 145 natural and health sciences journals tracked by the Nature Index. The New York metropolitan area, Guangzhou, Boston, San Francisco Bay Area, Wuhan, Hangzhou, and Baltimore-Washington rounded out the top 10 for 2025. Chinese cities strengthened their lead in the natural sciences overall, accounting for seven of the world's top 10 science cities in that field in 2025 — with Beijing, Shanghai, Nanjing, Guangzhou, Wuhan, Hangzhou, and Hefei placing first, second, third, fifth, sixth, eighth, and tenth respectively. By discipline, Beijing led rankings in chemistry, physical sciences, and Earth and environmental sciences, while the New York metropolitan area topped biological sciences. Beijing also maintained its leading position in natural sciences research output throughout 2016–2025; measured by adjusted Share, it recorded the fastest growth among cities worldwide during that period, followed by Shanghai and Guangzhou.
items.title: Chinese Cities Sweep Top Three in Nature Index Science Rankings

items.summary: November 26 is World Sustainable Transport Day, a UN initiative promoting safer, greener and better connected transport. The day carries added meaning in 2026, the first year of the UN Decade of Sustainable Transport (2026-2035). Reducing car dependence requires reliable public transit, safe cycling routes and seamless links between modes: Beijing lets riders bring bicycles onto select subway lines while a 14-kilometer Grand Canal greenway in Tongzhou District serves cyclists and walkers; Copenhagen aims for at least 75% of all trips to be made on foot, by bicycle or by public transport. Freight connectivity is also expanding — in January 2026 a freight train carrying Chongqing-made new energy vehicles departed Yuzui Station at Guoyuan Port bound for Nansha Port within 48 hours before transfer onto a vessel; and since trial operations began in 2012, Wuhan's China-Europe rail service has grown to 64 regular cross-border routes connecting 167 cities in 46 countries. The article notes that building sustainable transport requires more than infrastructure — reliable affordable services, safer accessible facilities, better mode coordination and closer international cooperation are all needed.
items.title: World Sustainable Transport Day Marks Start of UN Decade (2026-2035)

items.summary: The UK's Office for National Statistics reported that long-term international net migration fell to a provisional 77,000 in the year ending June 2026 (d2), more than half of the revised 204,000 recorded in YE June 2025 (q1/q4). Excluding pandemic years with travel restrictions, this is the lowest net migration estimate since 1997 (d3/d5) when surveys replaced administrative data. The ONS attributed the decline mainly to a steep fall in non-EU arrivals as visa rules tightened under both Conservative and Labour governments: provisional non-EU+ net migration dropped from 379,000 to 258,000 (d16), driven by immigration falling more than 100,000 while emigration stayed broadly stable. More Britons left the UK than arrived in YE June 2026 — an estimated 245,000 departures versus 109,000 arrivals (q17/q18) — and among EU-plus nationals more also departed (124,000 emigrating versus 79,000 immigrating; q20/q21), while the EU-27 plus Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Switzerland totalled 27 members (q19). The fall pushed net migration toward or below zero for British nationals (negative 137,000) and EU-plus nationals (negative 45,000), prompting reactions ranging from Labour's call for an immigration plan to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage disputing the figures by citing nearly a million net emigrants over ten years. The Guardian noted that David Cameron had set a target of below 100,000 before the 2010 election (d6/q7), which has now been achieved.
items.title: UK net migration falls to lowest since 1997 as it drops below zero

items.summary: At the European Council summit in Brussels, EU leaders remained deeply divided over the next multiannual budget and how to fund Ukraine. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said leaders were 'very far apart,' agreeing with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz that the current proposal was not viable because it is too large and insufficiently future-oriented; both called for a compromise before year-end, though Sweden's Ulf Kristersson suggested talks could drag into 2027 since the budget only takes effect in 2028. European Council President António Costa described securing an agreement as 'the most important' item but acknowledged it may not be possible this summit, hoping for a compromise by year-end; Irish PM Micheál Martin echoed that missing a deal before end of 2026 would make success in the first half of 2027 'very dim.' The core dispute centers on linking Ukraine support to the budget: Merz rejected any opt-out and insisted funding must come from all 27 member states, while Bulgaria's Rumen Radev agreed only to contribute €20bn toward non-military aid out of a proposed new €45bn loan. Four countries—Bulgaria, Czech Republic (PM Andrej Babiš), Hungary, and Slovakia—opposed the linkage, with Babiš arguing it is 'not possible' under the treaties and that cohesion spending should be negotiated separately; Kristersson accused them of trying to 'kidnap' Ukraine support. On Ukraine itself, Frederiksen warned that if Ukraine falls Russia could advance further, while Estonia's Kristen Michal cautioned that Ukraine would likely face a harsh winter and urged no budget cuts.
items.title: EU Leaders 'Very Far Apart' on Next Budget as Talks Stall Over Ukraine Funding

visual.alt: Bar chart. Total proposed new EU loan (to all members) (Loan total) 45,000,000,000 €; Bulgaria's contribution to non-military support only (Non-military) 20,000,000,000 €.

items.summary: Kenya's Cabinet Secretary for Mining and Blue Economy announced that the mining ministry has issued a notice of intention to award the tender for developing the Mrima Hill project to the U.S.-based consortium Frontier Minerals, according to Kenya's Ministry of Mining. The site is thought to be rich in critical minerals sought by electronics, aerospace, and energy industries; per the Kenyan ministry it holds at least 5.8 million tons (q1) of material that may contain niobium pentoxide, with two-thirds of the world's niobium reserves held by Brazil and the rest mostly China, plus potentially millions of metric tons of rare earth elements used in batteries, magnets, phones, and cars. The U.S. State Department said its interest reflects Washington's effort to diversify supply chains away from China while emphasizing transparency, local value addition, jobs, and economic benefits for both countries. However, Kenyan civil society organizations argue the process has not fully included local communities: Kenya's Ministry of Mining says a company must first obtain community consent before securing a license, yet in June 2026 (d2) the Centre for Litigation Trust filed a petition with the High Court in Kwale County alleging the agreement was
items.title: Kenya Issues Notice to Award Mrima Hill Mining Tender to U.S. Consortium

items.summary: In South Korea, where the birth rate is among the lowest in the world, families are spending heavily on premium baby products as their small number of children become what marketers call 'Very Important Babies' (VIBs). Mah Seungeun, a 38-year-old entrepreneur with one daughter, exemplifies this trend: because she has no siblings to share attention or expenses, each childhood milestone feels like a final opportunity. She notes that grandparents and other relatives also buy many gifts, reinforcing the spending pattern. This behavior is transforming South Korea into an unexpected market for high-end strollers, designer clothing, and toys.
items.title: South Korea's Low Birth Rate Fuels Premium Baby Goods Boom

items.summary: Two private screenings of the Pakistani television drama Dar-e-Nijaat (Door to Salvation) were cancelled in Bengaluru after an online backlash and police scrutiny. The events, one at a restaurant offering Persian and Arabic dinner with two episodes for a small ticket charge and another at a private theatre where guests were asked to dress in their 'best Pakistani ensemble,' had been promoted via social media before being called off by organizers who said they initially resisted cancelling but ultimately decided against proceeding.
items.title: Pakistani TV Drama Screenings Cancelled in India After Online Backlash

items.summary: Elon Musk pledged Wednesday that every child in the United States would receive two shares of SpaceX, doubling an October promise of one share each. The offer consists of a newly issued Class A share from SpaceX transferred through each child's Trump Account plus a matching personal share from Musk; SpaceX will transfer its shares in December while Musk plans to transfer his own in June 2027 when transfer restrictions expire. SpaceX raised about $85.7 billion (€78.4bn) at its June 2026 IPO, and the pledge's total value is unknown because it depends on both the share price and how many of the roughly 70 million Trump Accounts created by October are activated; at Wednesday's closing price of $127.44 per share (two shares worth $254.88), the offer would be worth about $17.8 billion (€16.3bn) if all 70 million accounts received both shares. To participate, parents or guardians must claim and activate their child's Trump Account; eligible US citizens born from 2025 through 2028 receive a one-off government contribution of $1,000 (€914), which is generally invested in low-cost funds tracking the US stock market with withdrawals usually restricted until the child turns 18. Musk said he recommends holding onto the shares and claimed SpaceX could reach about a million times the current global economy if it succeeds at making life multiplanetary and harnessing even a millionth of the Sun's energy, goals he called absurdly difficult but achievable.
items.title: Musk Doubles SpaceX Share Pledge to Every US Child

items.summary: Starbucks Korea is on track to return to profit in the fourth quarter after its first-ever quarterly loss, which came as boycotts mounted following a public-relations crisis over the controversial “Tank Day” promotion. The campaign offered discounts on large Tank series tumblers and sparked nationwide outrage because it coincided with the anniversary of the 1980 pro-democracy uprising that saw South Korea’s then-military junta deploy troops and tanks to crush protests, killing hundreds. E-Mart this month reported an earnings shock as Starbucks Korea’s third-quarter loss widened further before the anticipated recovery.
items.title: Starbucks Korea Posts Q4 Profit Recovery After 'Tank Day' Backlash

items.summary: Recent Ukrainian attacks on a Russian cargo vessel (the Sparta II) off Finland's coast and on the Russian corvette Merkury—along with an alleged weapons shipment near Libya—have drawn attention for occurring far from Ukraine. These operations followed suspected Russian missiles crashing in Poland, where an international military exercise was underway. Security expert Elisabeth Braw of the Atlantic Council said that unlike earlier shadow vessels simply transporting oil above a price cap, Sparta II was suspected of carrying military equipment, which Moscow denies; she noted this demonstrates Ukraine's ability to strike wherever and whatever waters Russian ships are in—something it could not do early in the war. Officially Kyiv aims to disrupt Russian logistics, but experts also read the strikes as political signals: Joachim Weber of the University of Bonn suggested Zelenskyy was sending a message of strength toward possible peace negotiations while paying less attention to the US out of disappointment. Analysts warn that if attacks on civilian or suspicious vessels in international waters increase—while Russia provides more escorts for its shadow fleet—the likelihood of an accidental exchange of fire rises, potentially making war omnipresent and undermining global maritime safety.
items.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Ships Far From Kyiv, Extending War to Baltic and Mediterranean

items.summary: Flight Centre has reported a cyber incident in which 'unknown persons' accessed customers' basic travel information along with a small number of passport details. The breach targeted a third-party accommodation system used by several of Flight Centre's booking agencies, exposing personal data held within that platform rather than the company's own systems directly. In response to the exposure, Flight Centre is warning affected customers to remain vigilant for unexpected emails or text messages concerning their bookings.
items.title: Flight Centre Data Breach Exposes Customer and Passport Details

items.summary: European Council President António Costa is meeting with leaders in Brussels to advance a deal on the EU's next seven-year budget, which he hopes to conclude by year's end. However, governments remain divided over spending levels and funding responsibilities, with priorities including support for farmers, addressing high housing and energy costs, and increased defence spending—particularly aid for Ukraine. European Parliament budget negotiator Carla Tavares told Euronews that the size of the budget is Parliament's primary concern; while she welcomed progress on new revenue sources such as a potential levy on large tech firms, she said she remains open to other funding options but warned that without additional revenue the EU would have to scale back its spending plans.
items.title: EU Budget Talks Stall Over Spending Priorities and Revenue Shortfalls

items.summary: Months after a rubbish landfill collapse killed dozens in the capital, Guinea has ordered residents of Conakry and its suburbs to conduct a mass clean-up. Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah announced on Wednesday a deadline of 31 December to clear rubbish across the city, relaying a directive from President Mamady Doumbouya. The order comes after heavy rains in August triggered a landslide at the capital's main waste dump that collapsed onto homes, killing 31 people and injuring others; the Dar es Salaam site was subsequently closed permanently, leaving piles of rubbish accumulating outside homes and on streets. Sanitation Minister Aboubacar Camara said Conakry generates about 3,000 tonnes of waste daily, with much ending up in the streets due to weaknesses in the collection system.
items.title: Guinea Orders Conakry Residents to Clean Up Capital by December After Deadly Landfill Collapse

items.summary: At the sixth China-Germany high-level security dialogue held in Berlin, CPC official Chen Wenqing discussed law enforcement and security cooperation with Nina Warken, head of the German Chancellery. Chen stated that China-Germany relations have maintained sound development momentum guided by consensus reached between President Xi Jinping and Germany's leadership, noting both countries share positions on upholding multilateralism and safeguarding regional peace and stability. He emphasized strengthening law enforcement and security cooperation to build a more just global governance system and consolidate the dialogue mechanism's outcomes through practical collaboration on mutual security concerns. Yin Bai, secretary general of the Commission for Political and Legal Affairs of the CPC Central Committee, co-chaired specialized exchanges with German counterparts during the event. Representatives from China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, Ministry of Public Security, Ministry of State Security, and People's Bank of China held in-depth discussions with their German equivalents on combating transnational organized crime, cybersecurity, and regional hotspot issues.
items.title: China-Germany Security Dialogue Focuses on Law Enforcement Cooperation

items.summary: The second press conference for the 2026 World Life Science Conference was held on Wednesday, November 25, at the Guangzhou Baiyun International Convention Center in Guangdong Province. The event is scheduled to run from November 28 to 30 and will welcome Nobel Prize laureates as well as recipients of the Lasker Award and Wolf Prize. It features 11 high-level keynote speeches on life sciences breakthroughs and 37 sub-forums covering topics including gene editing, AI-powered precision medicine, public health systems, and large-scale health governance. A dedicated session will examine pandemic risks, virus prevention, air pollution threats, big-data epidemiology, and how artificial intelligence can expand universal health coverage and improve equitable access to care. Another session titled 'Conversation with Women Scientists' invites researchers to discuss innovation, career development, challenges, turning points, and life choices, while students and early-career researchers are encouraged to participate directly. The conference aims to strengthen industry-academia-research collaboration in the Greater Bay Area by accelerating the translation of research into practical applications and supporting biopharmaceutical sector growth, with activities such as 'Nobel Laureates on Campus' bringing elite scientists to schools and the public.
items.title: 2026 World Life Science Conference Set for Guangzhou in November

items.summary: The UK Ministry of Defence sent letters to about 100,000 strategic reservists asking them to prepare for a possible call-up, media reported Thursday (26 November 2026). For the first time since the Cold War, these letters offered volunteers opportunities to take part in training and exercises. Signed by the heads of the Army, Navy and Royal Air Force, they also asked reservists to update their contact details and provide information about their current jobs and skills. The move comes amid reports that the Royal Air Force was moving aircraft into hangars overnight and planning anti-drone nets for British bases, following a Tuesday warning from MI5 and the Ministry of Defence that firms supplying Ukraine's military face increased sabotage risk from Russia. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting has stressed Britain must be ready to fight in 1,000 days, while the government recently announced £8 billion ($10.4 billion) in defense investment to improve submarine availability and readiness.
items.title: UK Ministry of Defence Sends Letters to About 100,000 Strategic Reservists on Possible Call-up

items.summary: A year after Labor's aged care overhaul took effect, a Senate committee into the Support at Home program has made 19 recommendations, including allowing clinicians to override assessment-algorithm outcomes. The committee found that elderly Australians' co-payments toward subsidised home services—ranging from 5% for some help up to 80% depending on service type and pension status—should be reviewed by the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing to assess impacts across incomes and needs and whether they discourage timely access to care. It also urged an immediate law change so humans can override algorithm outcomes at the point of assessment; currently only a government-run escalation pathway exists for exceptional circumstances. The committee delivered an interim report rather than its final one and has extended the inquiry until November next year, with Labor Senators saying they will hold their comments on the recommendations until then. Coalition and Greens figures united in criticism: Inquiry Chair Senator Penny Allman-Payne said Labor had botched the program, Shadow Aged Care Minister Anne Ruston called for human override to be restored now, and Centre Alliance MP Rebekha Sharkie questioned why aged care was underspent by $1.4 billion last financial year—part of a $44 billion budget that has effectively doubled since 2022.
items.title: Senate committee recommends review of Support at Home co-payments and algorithm override

items.summary: The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency announced Wednesday that its operatives seized over $220 million worth of methamphetamine and arrested five Mexican suspects at an industrial-scale laboratory in Enugu State. According to agency spokesman Femi Babafemi, the Mexicans were allegedly recruited by a Nigerian national before entering Nigeria with forged passports; one attempt was denied based on intelligence about their alleged plans, while a second crossing using forged Benin passports succeeded until authorities alerted officials and monitored them for weeks. The suspects were arrested at the Enugu lab on November 11. This seizure is among the largest this year in a country that has become an emerging hub for illegal drugs, following a transnational drug syndicate involving Nigerians and Mexicans busted in southwestern Nigeria in May. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime attributes West and Central Africa's rise as a major center for global illicit drug trafficking and manufacturing to porous borders and corruption.
items.title: Nigeria Seizes $220 Million in Methamphetamine, Arrests Five Mexican Suspects

items.summary: A huge explosion at the Bangchak oil depot in eastern Bangkok on Thursday sent a large fireball and thick black smoke into the sky, injuring seven people — four classified as critical and three less severe. The blast was so powerful it rattled doors several kilometres away, according to AFP reporters who witnessed a column of flames followed by dense black smoke. Bangna District Office urged nearby residents to evacuate immediately after an explosion occurred at the facility.
items.title: Bangkok Oil Depot Explosion Injures Seven and Sends Fireball Into Sky

items.summary: Illegal gold mining is intensifying across several West African states, exposing the difficulty of governing their mineral resources and raising questions about sector governance. In Guinea's Siguiri prefecture, where open-pit alluvial mining using heavy machinery continued despite a July 2025 ban, 139 officials were suspended for violations; 22 former territorial administrators were convicted of pollution complicity but acquitted on corruption and money-laundering charges because investigations stopped at the pits without tracing financial flows. The state also inaugurated a refinery with an announced capacity of more than 700 tonnes per year while exporting only 70 tonnes of gold in 2025, prompting about 160,000 people to flee into Mali. In Burkina Faso, since the national precious-substances agency SONASP began buying artisanal gold, declared volumes rose from under half a tonne annually to nearly 29 tonnes in the first half of 2026; elsewhere, armed groups such as JNIM fill security gaps left by states that ban mining without permanent presence. In Senegal's Kédougou region, the army destroyed 32 dredges but operations recur because a 2024 decree suspends activity only on the Senegalese side of the Falémé River while about six to seven tonnes of gold escape the state annually as miners sell in better-paying Mali. In Mali, between 2013 and 2022, authorities declared 37.7 tonnes of exports to the United Arab Emirates against 672 tonnes recorded there — a gap worth roughly $27.6 billion attributed by researcher Soumaïla Lah's study (covering 2022–2026) to fragmented institutions whose overlapping competences keep gold statistically invisible; he argues that designating a lead authority and exchanging customs data with the UAE would improve control.
items.title: West African States Struggle to Curb Illegal Gold Mining

items.summary: Brazilian criminal forensic scientist Alexandre Deitos is trying to identify the bodies of African migrants who died aboard a boat that washed ashore in Mauritania after drifting across the Atlantic. Analyzing 28 mobile phones and two IDs recovered from the vessel, his team concluded it had originated in West Africa carrying migrants toward Europe before going off course for weeks. To match DNA samples with relatives, Deitos traveled more than 1,500 kilometres across the Sahara over 10 days to collect samples from 85 people; this effort helped confirm the death of Souleimane Gassama and allowed Kadiatou, his wife in Mauritania, to finally receive confirmation. Separately, grieving father Kouna Cissé found peace after recognizing an X-ray of a broken ankle taken by Brazilian authorities that matched one from 2020 for his son Sidy, whose death is still awaiting formal verification. Deitos's team has identified six of the nine bodies recovered and believes at least 42 men boarded the vessel, though the total passenger count remains unknown.
items.title: Brazilian forensic scientist identifies migrants on 'ghost ships'

items.summary: On November 25, South Korea's benchmark KOSPI index fell 6.16%, shedding 308.52 points to close at 4,697.51 — its lowest closing level since January 13 and one of the steepest single-day declines of the year. The sharp reversal followed a strong rally on November 24 when the index had gained 4.79% amid renewed enthusiasm for AI stocks after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returned to his role; selling then intensified as falling US chip stocks and reports that Washington could impose fresh tariffs on 16 economies weighed on investor sentiment. The market's two largest semiconductor companies bore much of the damage: Samsung Electronics shares fell 9.87% and SK Hynix plunged 11.05%. During a live broadcast, financial television anchor Kim Ah-hyun struggled to hold back tears as she watched a chart showing a Samsung Electronics-linked leveraged investment product plunge more than 15% in the session (a specific figure of 15.21% appeared on screen). She described her reaction as 'tears of anger' after hearing repeated accounts of retail investors suffering substantial losses, and urged them not to lose hope. The incident prompted South Korean authorities to consider additional market support: reports indicate the government is examining an expansion of its securities market stabilisation fund — which currently stands at 10.76 trillion won, or around $8 billion — after Korea Development Bank reportedly approached 25 financial institutions to assess their capacity to contribute more funds; no final decision has been announced. The KOSPI recovered the next day on November 26, rising 0.3% to close at 4,711.21 as Samsung Electronics gained 0.4% and SK Hynix advanced 2.2%.
items.title: South Korean TV Anchor Breaks Down on Air as KOSPI Crashes

items.summary: The Nifty IT index climbed 2.25 per cent to close at 32,932.85 on Thursday (November 26, 2026), adding 725.30 points from its previous close of 32,207.55 as seven of its ten constituents advanced. HCLTech led the gainers with a 4.67 per cent rise to ₹1,444.50, followed by Wipro up 3.53 per cent to ₹195.73 and Infosys gaining 3.38 per cent to ₹1,168.20; TCS rose 2.92 per cent while Tech Mahindra added 1.65 per cent. Coforge was the steepest decliner at minus 3.88 per cent, and Mphasis slipped 1.43 per cent. The index opened at 32,514.25 and reached an intraday high of 33,037.05 against a low of 32,494.35.
items.title: Nifty IT index rose over 2% as HCLTech and Wipro led the rally

visual.alt: Bar chart. HCLTech 4.67 %; Wipro 3.53 %; Infosys 3.38 %; TCS 2.92 %; Tech Mahindra 1.65 %; LTM 1.33 %; Persistent 0.36 %; Oracle Financial Services Software 0.03 %.

items.summary: According to a Financial Times report published Thursday (November 26, 2026), Nvidia has instructed its manufacturing partners—including Dell and Supermicro—to stop shipping servers containing its chips into four Southeast Asian countries: Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia. The FT cited three people with knowledge of the matter for this account. Under these instructions, packaging companies told buyers in those nations that their orders would not be shipped because Nvidia will not permit them to proceed. Reuters could not immediately verify the report, and Nvidia, Dell, and Supermicro did not respond to comment requests outside regular business hours. The FT added that it is unclear whether the halt is temporary while Nvidia and its partners work out how to comply with new US export controls.
items.title: Nvidia Halts Chip Shipments to Southeast Asia

items.summary: Following Michael Dell's disclosure that more than 90% of the investment accounts he and his wife funded for 25 million American children remain unclaimed, Elon Musk and SpaceX announced a stock donation initiative aimed at encouraging participation in the program. According to CNBC, SpaceX will donate one newly issued Class A share to every active Trump Account, with CEO Elon Musk personally matching each donated share; separately, SpaceX President and COO Gwynne Shotwell pledged over 2 million shares of her own. On X, Musk said the company's shares would transfer next month while his personal shares would follow after his lock-up expires in June next year, noting that if SpaceX achieves its long-term goals it could be worth about a million times the current global economy and advising holders to keep their shares. The initiative comes as the White House reported nearly 70 million Trump Accounts created (more than 60 million through automatic enrollment), though officials have not disclosed how many remain active, while total program deposits since its July 4 launch surpassed $9 billion including more than $1 billion from families and friends.
items.title: SpaceX and Musk Pledge Shares to Active Trump Accounts After Michael Dell's Warning

items.summary: In a review of Vivo's latest flagship, the X500 Pro Max is positioned as a photography-focused phone that also courts Apple users. Technology Editor Vishal Mathur (Hindustan Times) describes it as pairing a stabilised 200-megapixel zoom lens with restrained, true-to-life Zeiss colour science and claims this
items.title: Vivo X500 Pro Max Pairs a Stabilised 200-Megapixel Zoom Lens with Zeiss Colour Science

items.summary: Jay Puri, a longtime Nvidia executive who led its global sales team and joined the company in 2005 after two decades at Sun Microsystems, is facing scrutiny over his relationship with Cenly Chen, former chief growth officer of server maker Super Micro. The couple dated for several years and married on March 7 this year according to records, and their ties have come under investigation amid a US probe into allegations that Super Micro servers loaded with Nvidia chips were diverted to China.
items.title: Nvidia Chief's Aide Jay Puri's Romance With Super Micro Executive Amid China Chip Diversion Probe

items.summary: IBM announced it will stop sponsoring green cards and U.S. work visas for most roles in its IBM Consulting division, asking affected employees to relocate abroad or resign by December 31. The company cited changing business requirements and the availability of skilled workers as reasons; an IBM spokesperson said participation in U.S. high-skilled visa programs has been declining over years while skill availability and client needs have evolved. IBM Consulting is described as its largest division, employing over 150,000 employees globally (q1). The company reportedly gave affected employees three weeks to decide on relocation, offered those who do not relocate three months' severance with a final working day of December 31, and has not disclosed how many employees are likely affected or currently based in the U.S. This decision comes amid tightened U.S. employment-based immigration rules under the Trump administration, which proposed a USD 100,000 fee for certain new H-1B petitions (q2) alongside changes favoring higher-paid positions.
items.title: IBM to End US Visa Sponsorship for Most Consulting Roles

items.summary: Chhattisgarh police arrested two members of an interstate gang, including its alleged kingpin Safan Khan (35), in connection with the theft of Apple products worth nearly ₹2 crore from a store operated by iNext Innovation Pvt Ltd at Marine Drive in Raipur's Telibandha area during the night of October 31 to November 1. The gang broke open the shutter and stole 173 iPhones, along with Apple Watches, headphones, AirPods, and the CCTV DVR. Police recovered 125 stolen iPhones valued at around ₹1.5 crore from Julwania in Madhya Pradesh's Barwani district after Safan Khan disclosed information during questioning. The arrested men were identified as Rajesh Ajay Singh Jhala alias Jhala (43), a resident of Tonk Khurd in Dewas district, and Safan Khan; two others, including Jhala's son Raj Jhala and Rajesh Lodhi, remain absconding. Investigators formed six special teams with more than 40 personnel who analysed over 1,000 CCTV recordings along a route spanning nearly 250 km, examined data from over 1,100 cell-ID towers and more than 10 lakh mobile numbers, and tracked the suspects for nearly 10 days. Police are also investigating whether the gang arranged thefts at high-end Apple stores across the country and disposed of stolen phones in Bangladesh and Nepal.
items.title: Two Kanjar Gang Members Arrested in ₹2 Crore Raipur Apple Store Theft; 125 iPhones Recovered

items.summary: On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance downplayed the likelihood that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang would require a presidential pardon ahead of his scheduled congressional testimony. Citing confirmations from Justice Department officials and multiple national security officials, Vance stated that Huang is 'under no investigation' and asserted he had seen no evidence that Huang committed a crime, leaving any prosecution to relevant authorities. The remarks followed President Donald Trump's statement to the New York Post on Tuesday that pardoning Huang was 'always an option,' though not necessary; Trump also expressed his preference that Huang not invoke Fifth Amendment rights when testifying. Huang is expected to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview with House Intelligence and Foreign Affairs committees and the Select Committee on China on Dec. 1, followed by a public Senate Banking Committee hearing on Dec. 3. The situation has drawn scrutiny over the intersection of business and politics amid Nvidia's board reversal in reinstating Huang after his resignation over acknowledged extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed suspected of ties to China's Ministry of State Security—claims Beijing denies. Congressional intelligence committee staffers received a classified briefing on Tuesday from officials representing the CIA, FBI, and Office of the Director of National Intelligence. Trump has credited his administration for pressuring Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang, asserting that his administration assured company officials Huang did not pose a national security risk, while Vance emphasized that individuals are tried based on evidence rather than anonymously sourced reporting.
items.title: Vance Says Jensen Huang Needs No Presidential Pardon

items.summary: According to a report by the Financial Times, Nvidia has instructed its manufacturing partners—including Dell and Supermicro—to stop shipping computer servers containing its AI chips to buyers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia. The British newspaper cited three people with knowledge of the matter but noted it was unclear whether the halt is temporary. Buyers affected include Aolani, a Singapore-based cloud computing company that had planned to lease Nvidia hardware to ByteDance, owner of Chinese TikTok; AFP has contacted all five companies for comment. An executive at a cloud provider told the newspaper that Washington's new rules caused "sheer chaos" during the 90-day window in which buyers must apply for newly required licenses. The report comes after US export controls on Nvidia advanced chips—first imposed since 2022 and recently tightened to close loopholes around chip smuggling and grey-market rentals from data centers in third countries, often in Southeast Asia—and amid an espionage scandal that forced longtime CEO Jensen Huang out before his reinstatement on Sunday. That scandal reportedly stems from allegations involving Alice Huang's affair with Jensen Huang; she is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company under investigation for allegedly transferring Nvidia chips to China in circumvention of US rules, and some US officials suspect her of spying for Beijing. Separately, KPMG projects that data center capacity in Southeast Asia will triple from 2025 levels by 2030 as AI use surges tenfold.
items.title: Nvidia Halts Server Shipments to Four Southeast Asian Nations

items.summary: Elon Musk pledged two SpaceX shares for every child in the United States, doubling an offer he made last month and combining one share from SpaceX with one held personally by him. At SpaceX's Wednesday closing price of $127.44 per share (per Forbes), Axios estimated the gift would be worth about $18 billion—roughly triple Michael Dell's once record-breaking contribution to Trump Accounts—and roughly three times his October pledge, based on U.S. census figures of about 72 million minors. Because Musk owns billions of SpaceX shares and the company has billions outstanding, the giveaway is unlikely to materially affect him or other investors; his stake was about 6.42 billion shares as of June (per Axios). The Wednesday pledge follows an October 19 promise of one share per child next year and a same-day SpaceX announcement committing newly issued Class A shares to children with Trump Accounts, which Musk said he would match. No timeline for the broader U.S.-wide distribution was given; SpaceX would transfer its share in December and his personal share is expected to follow in June 2026, though it remains unclear whether the full pledge will be delivered through Trump Accounts. This mirrors a July offer by Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president and COO, who pledged one share each to 2 million Trump Accounts alongside her husband. The pledge arrives as SpaceX shares have fallen about 13 percent since Musk's first promise amid a broader sell-off in AI-linked stocks, meaning the gift is now worth less than it would have been at the October price.
items.title: Elon Musk Doubles SpaceX Share Pledge to Every U.S. Child

items.summary: The rupee strengthened sharply, closing at an eight-month high of 92.2337 per dollar as most other Asian currencies weakened on Wednesday, extending a November run fueled by record foreign equity inflows and lower oil prices after rebounding from near-record lows the previous month. Banks see further upside: ANZ Banking Group sees room for the rupee to gain to 90-91 per dollar (q1-q2), ICICI Securities Primary Dealership expects it to reach at least 91, about 1.4% stronger than its current level (q3), and Barclays Plc recommends a three-month offshore bet on the rupee against the dollar targeting 89.53 (q4). The swift rebound gives the Reserve Bank of India an opportunity to recoup foreign-exchange reserves that have fallen by more than $80 billion from their September peak (q6); meanwhile, the authority's record $239.2 billion short forward book also adds to the case for buying dollars (q7). HDFC Bank principal economist Sakshi Gupta noted that a slightly prolonged period of rupee appreciation could be necessary before hedging behavior changes and may give the central bank reason not to soak up dollar inflows aggressively at present.
items.title: Analysts See Room for Rupee to Strengthen Before RBI Intervention

items.summary: Haryanvi singer Sapna Choudhary, who gained fame through Bigg Boss 11, confirmed she has filed for divorce from husband Veer Sahu after six years of marriage; the couple shares two children. Her Instagram account subsequently disappeared, displaying a message that the page is unavailable and may have been removed or deactivated, though the reason remains unknown to observers. This development followed Veer's announcement of his upcoming album titled Prince & Prostitute, whose poster depicts him shirtless with long hair while an unidentified woman stands behind him holding him from the back. In a recent interview with NMF News, Sapna addressed public curiosity about their marriage, stating that when things were good they stayed together and now that things are not good they have separated, emphasizing that marriage is between two people who will decide what to do privately rather than allowing others to interfere.
items.title: Sapna Choudhary's Instagram Account Disappears After Husband Announces New Album Amid Divorce

items.summary: The Trump administration has proposed a contingent tariff rate of 17% on India, provided New Delhi reaches a trade deal. This rate is described as slightly lower than the rates planned for several countries with which India competes, potentially giving Indian exporters a competitive edge. Specifically, the US proposes an 18% rate for Bangladesh, Cambodia and Indonesia; a 20% rate for Vietnam if it strikes a trade deal; and a 20% rate for China under a truce that expires on January 10 (rising to 40% if that truce collapses). The proposed Indian rate sits above the current global baseline of 10%, which Trump imposed through emergency powers, but below the maximum punitive level of up to 100% reserved for India over its Russian oil purchases. Trade negotiations began in February 2025 and have yet to conclude amid disputes over trade practices and a new US law tied to Indian crude imports.
items.title: India's Proposed 17% Tariff Is Lower Than Rivals' Rates

items.summary: The Trump administration proposed up to 25% tariffs on Indian imports (q1), which would fall to 17% if New Delhi and Washington finalize the long-pending trade deal they agreed an interim framework for in February at 18% (q3). This proposal stems from a USTR Section 301 investigation into India's manufacturing policies, structural excess capacity claims—which India has rejected—and market-access barriers (q5, q14). The proposed duty is net of existing tariffs and would not be added to the separate 10% forced-labour tariff imposed since July 24; importers pay the higher of the two rates (q9). Among the 14 economies targeted in this fresh round—China, EU, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India—the proposed 17% rate for India sits below those planned for several key competitors: 18% for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand (q12), and 20% for China and Vietnam (q13). This could give Indian exporters a competitive edge. Rival rates vary elsewhere: Vietnam faces up to 35% without a deal versus 20% with one (q19); China's 20% aligns with a US-China truce expiring January 10, rising to 40% if it unravels; and the EU, Japan, and Switzerland face 15%, including MFN duties. The new tariffs are not expected to take effect until next year after public consultation and hearings—written comments due by January 5, 2027 (d10), with hearings beginning January 25.
items.title: Trump Tariffs: India Faces Up to 25% US Duty, Below Rivals With a Trade Deal

visual.alt: Bar chart. India 17 %; Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand 18 %; China and Vietnam (with deal) 20 %; EU, Japan, Switzerland 25 %.

items.summary: The Trump administration announced new tariffs on Thursday targeting 14 economies that together account for roughly half of the global economy. These duties follow a months-long Section 301 probe in which USTR Jamieson Greer concluded that these countries' manufacturing practices relating to excess capacity and production are 'unreasonable and burden or restrict US commerce.' China, facing a 20 per cent tariff, dismissed the overcapacity rationale as a 'false premise,' while Japan faces up to 15 per cent in new duties. Singapore, due for a 20 per cent rate, called itself 'very disappointed' with the proposal, and Malaysia denied having excess manufacturing capacity that distorts global markets. The countries protested Washington's allegations of structural excess production capacity, though Thailand found its capped 18 per cent tariff more favourable than expected.
items.title: China, Japan and Other US Trade Partners Reject Trump Tariffs Over Excess Capacity

items.summary: The North Central Railway (NCR) has warned its employees against creating and posting social media reels during duty hours, stating that the activity distracts staff and jeopardises train operations. The railway zone also flagged the possibility of employees earning money through such content, cautioning that this could amount to running an unauthorised commercial enterprise or side business. Additionally, NCR clarified that any employee producing educational or awareness-related content about the Railways would need prior approval from the competent authority.
items.title: North Central Railway Warns Staff Against Making Social Media Reels During Duty

items.summary: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge broke his silence Thursday on Samajwadi Party MP Imran Masood's aggressive criticism of the party over seat-sharing in Uttar Pradesh, advising him at a Lucknow event to 'focus on action rather than just words.' The remarks come as friction grows between Congress and its INDIA bloc ally SP ahead of the 2027 assembly elections. Masood questioned the rationale behind continuing seat-sharing discussions after Akhilesh Yadav-led SP announced five candidates while negotiations with Congress were still ongoing, arguing that an alliance requires joint decisions rather than one partner leaving seats for another. He insisted he would not accept a subordinate position and declined to comment on the SP's manifesto scheduled for release later Thursday. His latest remarks followed earlier attacks in which Masood questioned whether SP wanted to fight BJP or its ally, compared Congress to zero, and threatened to 'fight back' if treated as servants rather than partners. A senior SP functionary told The Times of India that either the Congress leadership was ignoring these statements or unaware of them, suggesting neither interpretation is positive for the alliance.
items.title: Kharge Urges Masood to Focus on Action Amid SP Friction

items.summary: A study of nearly four decades of Indian fisheries data finds that sardine and anchovy landings are tied to large-scale climate oscillations, sea-surface temperatures, and coastal winds. Researchers from the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), Pune, analysed annual landing records from 1981 to 2019 in the Indian exclusive economic zone using data from fisheries surveys conducted by the Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute (CMFRI). Small pelagic fish—Indian oil sardine and anchovies—showed alternating periods of higher and lower abundance over several decades, with the oil sardine appearing in three-to-four-year cycles. Anchovies moved out of phase with sardines: a sardine recovery followed an anchovy decline by three to four years, while a subsequent anchovy recovery was followed by a sardine decline after a similar period; however, this recurring relationship does not establish that either species causes changes in the other.
