Sardine and anchovy landings showed stronger relationships with global sea-surface temperatures than other groups—higher landings were associated with a negative phase of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) and positive North Atlantic temperatures at decadal timescales—and sardine variability was also linked to northward winds along India's west coast. The study found a significant decline in shark catch of about 0.4 kilotonnes per year, which did not show clear associations with the climate variables analysed; Hamza notes this should be interpreted as a combination of fisheries and ecological signals rather than quantified causes. These findings align with globally observed sardine-anchovy regime shifts but do not establish simple causal relationships between climate and fish catches, since landings are not direct measurements of abundance and can change with recruitment, fishing effort, behaviour, and local conditions.
items.title: Indian Sardine and Anchovy Landings Linked to Large-Scale Climate Drivers

items.summary: The Supreme Court said on Thursday it would examine whether accredited journalists enjoy greater protection than 'self-proclaimed' journalists while covering protests, per Bar and Bench. The court was hearing petitions filed by the Kerala Union of Working Journalists over Delhi Police's alleged illegal detentions and forcible removal of journalists covering October protests in New Delhi demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar; those protests were organized by the Cockroach Janta Party political campaign, Opposition parties, and student groups. The bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana disposed of a plea about the alleged detention and manhandling of seven journalists, sending it to a court-appointed inquiry committee that had been formed on August 20 following July youth protests. On Thursday, the court asked what qualifies as a journalist and whether professional accreditation or institutional affiliation should determine protection for those covering protests, quoting itself as asking 'Do journalists enjoy any special privilege vis-à-vis law enforcement agencies while covering protests?' It also raised whether forcible removal of a journalist from a protest site amounts to custody and what constitutional consequences such an act carries. The bench observed that journalistic freedom must be balanced with the need to maintain public order, and said it would examine larger constitutional questions while individual allegations of police excesses are reviewed by the inquiry committee.
items.title: Supreme Court to Examine Whether Accredited Journalists Get Greater Protection Than Self-Proclaimed Ones During Protests

items.summary: The trilateral Russia–China–US meeting held in Shenzhen on November 19 concluded with a four-point joint statement called the 'Declaration toward Peace,' which addressed UN reform, stable energy flows after the Strait of Hormuz blockade, state consent and opposition to International Criminal Court jurisdiction overreach, and nuclear non-proliferation—but deliberately omitted any reference to artificial intelligence regulation. The article argues this omission reflects converging strategic interests between AI rivals: while the US holds roughly 72 per cent of global AI computing capacity accumulated since 2022 (per Epoch AI estimates), China is the leading source of global AI research talent, with an estimated 11 per cent rise in Chinese-origin researchers to more than 2,100 people added by one industry estimate in 2025. The two nations also differ in approach—the US leads foundational platforms like ChatGPT (launched in 2022) while China has moved faster on AI deployment across its economy—and both are wary of regulating military use of AI, even as Stockholm International Peace Research Institute's 2025 research warns that AI-enabled applications could compress decision-making timelines and increase nuclear escalation risk. The piece also notes India's position in the race, citing Google's data-centre campus in Visakhapatnam with reported investment figures ranging from $6 billion to $15 billion across different announcements.
items.title: Russia, China and the US left AI out of their Shenzhen peace declaration

items.summary: A collection of reader responses to several Scroll articles. One commenter described observing an 'irrational' village school in Balaghat where the management committee ate snacks without discussing issues, students stopped asking questions due to tuition dependence and rote learning, special-needs children were treated as if not human, Sanskrit was prioritised over mother tongue, and science and maths were neglected because teachers were busy with election and Census work. A separate commenter questioned factual claims in a book about Sonia Gandhi's relationship with Rajiv Gandhi, asking how she could have watched the 2002 demolition of the Babri Masjid live given that the Godhra train carnage occurred after their return from Ayodhya. Other readers weighed in on civic behaviour and leadership norms, disputed reports of anti-India content by citing alleged foreign funding, argued against equal rights for Overseas Citizen of India cardholders while questioning why courts remained silent when Narendra Modi participated in election propaganda favouring Donald Trump, praised an article about the Almora Literature Festival as a means to preserve Kumauni culture and local literature, and called for literary awards' cash prizes to match their prestige. Regarding prize money, one commenter noted that the Nobel Prize carries 12 million Swedish kronor; the Booker Prize offers £50,000 split between author and translator; the Pulitzer Award gives $15,000; Indian awards such as the Sahitya Akademi award provide Rs 50,000 to Rs 1 lakh with a shawl; and some prizes like the Jnanpith were recently increased to Rs 11 lakh cash.
items.title: Scroll readers' comments on Indian education, caste politics and literary awards

items.summary: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Abhijeet Dipke and Ashutosh Ranka have reportedly been issued lookout notices in connection with first information reports registered after an October 2 protest held without permission at Shivaji Park in Dadar, Mumbai. Separately, CJP leader Saurav Das moved the Delhi High Court after immigration officials stopped him from boarding a flight to the United Kingdom at Delhi airport; the Centre told Justice Amit Mahajan that a lookout circular had been issued against Das at the request of Mumbai Police over discrepancies in his passport records concerning his schooling, address and parentage. Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma said these discrepancies could also raise questions about Das's Indian citizenship but noted he could not provide a copy of the circular or disclose when it was issued, stating that Das could challenge it in separate proceedings. Senior advocate Akhil Sibal argued on behalf of Das that his client received a show-cause notice only after reaching the airport and questioned how citizens should be treated without being told about such restrictions.
items.title: Lookout Notices Issued Against CJP Leaders Over Prohibited Mumbai Protest

items.summary: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge launched a sharp attack on the BJP and RSS during a 'Samvidhan Raksha' march in Lucknow on Constitution Day, accusing them of spreading hatred, undermining the Constitution over the past 12 years, and questioning Congress leaders' patriotism. He likened the two organizations to people whose bite could be fatal —
items.title: Kharge Attacks BJP and RSS at Lucknow Constitution Day Rally
